name: Niger Delta
summary: Africa's largest wetland delta where the Niger meets the Atlantic; Nigeria's petroleum heartland.
description: The delta covers ~70,000 km² of mangrove, freshwater swamp, and barrier islands. It holds the bulk of Nigeria's oil and gas, a dense creek network, and highly politicised environmental and federal-revenue issues.
elevationNote: Mostly near sea level; tidal mangrove
character: Mangrove, oilfields, riverine settlements, barrier islands.
economy: Oil and gas, fisheries, boat transport, refining.
agriculture: Hydromorphic gleysols, peat, and alluvial deposits on a landscape of seasonally flooded flats, backswamps, and levees. Oil-palm agroforest dominates the better-drained levee ridges; fisheries are economically vital.
crops: Oil palm (Elaeis guineensis) — the delta is the heart of Nigeria's smallholder oil-palm belt; red palm oil and kernel extraction
Rubber (Hevea brasiliensis) — plantation and smallholder rubber on drier ridges (Edo, Delta)
Plantain and banana (Musa spp.) — staple carbohydrate on levee soils
Cassava — garri, lafun, and fufu processing across the delta hinterland
Yam — white and yellow yam in the drier northern delta fringe
Rice — both lowland swamp rice and fadama irrigation (Rivers, Delta State paddies)
Cocoyam (Colocasia & Xanthosoma) — shade-tolerant tuber under palm canopy
Fluted pumpkin (Telfairia occidentalis) — ugu leaf vegetable widely intercropped
Vegetables: amaranth, okra, peppers, garden egg — backyard and creek bank gardens
Coconut palm — barrier beaches and island fringes of the delta mouth
Mangrove (Rhizophora, Avicennia) — fuelwood, poles, and fisheries habitat
Fish, shrimp, and crab artisanal fisheries — the delta is Nigeria's richest inland/coastal fishery
planting: Plant cassava and yam on levee ridges (higher drained ground) away from deep backswamps
Oil palms are usually retained on family farms — propagate by seedling and suckers at 9×9 m spacing
Use mounds and raised beds for vegetables in perennially waterlogged backswamp soils
Construct small fish ponds (earthen ponds) in abandoned rice fields for tilapia and catfish
Avoid draining mangrove wetlands — nursery habitat for fish stocks and shoreline protection

name: Sokoto Basin
summary: Semi-arid sedimentary basin of the northwest drained by the Sokoto–Rima system.
description: Cretaceous–Tertiary sediments underlie millet, sorghum, and irrigated fadama. The basin is drought-prone and depends on dams and groundwater. It is the core landscape of the Caliphate northwest.
character: Sahel–Sudan plains, seasonal rivers, irrigation schemes.
economy: Grain, livestock, onions (dry-season irrigation), limited oil exploration historically.

name: Guinea Savanna
summary: Wooded savanna belt between southern rainforest and northern Sudan/Sahel savanna.
description: Guinea savanna (southern and northern Guinea) is Nigeria's broad middle belt: shea, yam, sorghum, and cattle routes. Rainfall is typically 900–1,500 mm. It includes much of Kwara, Niger, Kogi, Benue, Nasarawa, and parts of Kaduna and FCT.
character: Parkland trees, seasonal burn, mixed farming.
economy: Yam, shea, grains, livestock corridors, Abuja hinterland.
agriculture: Deep ferric luvisols support root crops and cereals. Shea parklands are retained on farm fields across the belt. Short fallow rotations are common.
crops: Yam (Dioscorea rotundata) — white guinea yam is the staple tuber crop
Cassava (Manihot esculenta) — processed into garri, fufu, and flour
Guinea corn / Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) — guinea-corn for ogi, pap, and tuwo
Millet (Pennisetum glaucum) — early-maturing dry-season staple
Maize (Zea mays) — grown as second crop in yam/cassava rotations
Rice (Oryza sativa & O. glaberrima) — lowland fadama and upland varieties
Shea nut (Vitellaria paradoxa) — shea butter extraction, parkland agroforestry
Groundnut / Peanut (Arachis hypogaea) — oilseed and snack crop
Soybean (Glycine max) — expanding for oil and poultry feed
Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) — beans and leaves as vegetable
Sesame (Sesamum indicum) — northern guinea fringe for oilseeds
Mango, citrus, and cashew — scattered commercial orchards
planting: Plant yam mounds (heaps) with stakes from November–December; seed yam setts planted February–April
Sorghum and millet sown at first rains (April–May); late maize July–August
Cassava stem cuttings planted March–May, harvested 9–18 months later
Shea trees retained as permanent parkland — do not clear mature shea on new farms
Use minimum tillage and tied ridges to reduce runoff on sloping ground

name: Sudan Savanna
summary: Open-tree savanna of the far-north fringe — drier than Guinea, main cereal and legume zone.
description: Sudan savanna is Nigeria's northern crop-and-livestock belt with 500–900 mm annual rainfall, shorter wet season (3–5 months), and scattered acacia and baobab trees. It covers most of Kano, Katsina, southern Sokoto, southern Borno, Jigawa, Bauchi and Gombe.
elevationNote: Mostly 350–700 m undulating plains with inselbergs
character: Acacia parkland, baobab, seasonal wadis, transhumance cattle corridors.
economy: Cereals, legumes, livestock, irrigation dams, dry-season onion belts.
agriculture: Shallow sandy-loam soils with low organic matter — rely on organic manure, mulch, and small-scale irrigation (tudun wada fadamas). Wind erosion and desertification pressures on the northern fringe.
crops: Millet (Pennisetum glaucum) — early and extra-early varieties dominate (doro, maiwa)
Guinea corn / Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) — tall late varieties on deeper soils
Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) — dual-purpose grain and leaves (dan wake)
Groundnut (Arachis hypogaea) — historic groundnut pyramid belt (Kano, Katsina)
Sesame (Sesamum indicum) — Jigawa, Bauchi, Gombe are leading producers
Wheat (Triticum aestivum) — irrigated dry season on Hadejia-Jama'are fadamas
Onion (Allium cepa) — dry-season irrigated bulb crop (Aliero riba, Kano red)
Tomato & pepper — irrigated dry season vegetables, especially Kano/Jigawa
Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) — orange-fleshed varieties expanding
Baobab (Adansonia digitata) — fruit, leaves (kuka), and bark for traditional uses
Acacia gum (Acacia senegal) — gum arabic agroforestry on the fringe
Neem (Azadirachta indica) — multipurpose shade, medicinal, and windbreak tree
planting: Sow millet and sorghum at first effective rains (June–early July); use tied ridges to capture moisture
Intercrop cowpea with millet/sorghum to reduce erosion risk and maximise land
Dry-season onion and tomato: plant on raised beds October–November, irrigate through March
Construct small earthen bunds and zaï pits on degraded soils to capture runoff
Retain baobab, acacia, and faidherbia trees in farm fields for soil fertility and fodder

name: Sahel Savanna
type: Semi-arid vegetation belt at the desert fringe
summary: Semi-arid grass and acacia steppe on the northern desert boundary — pastoral and resilient dry-crop zone.
description: The Sahel is the narrow northernmost vegetation zone along the Niger border with <500 mm annual rainfall and frequent droughts. It is dominated by short grass, sparse acacia, and a pastoral economy based on cattle, sheep, and goats. Lake Chad and Komadougu-Yobe basins sustain irrigation oasis.
elevationNote: 250–450 m; flat to gently rolling sandy plains
character: Short annual grass, scattered thorny trees, wadis, transhumance routes and lake oases.
economy: Pastoralism, drought-millet, lake-basin irrigation, gum arabic agroforestry.
agriculture: Very fragile sandy soils with low water-holding capacity — depend on drought-tolerant crops, water-harvesting structures, and lake/fadama irrigation. Desertification and wind erosion are active challenges.
crops: Drought millet (Pennisetum glaucum) — extra-early 60-day varieties (zuru, sara)
Sorghum (early-maturing drought types) — occasionally with supplemental watering
Cowpea — drought-tolerant black-eyed varieties for grain and fodder
Wheat — around Lake Chad pump-irrigation and Komadougu floodplain
Dryland rice — Oryza glaberrima on fadamas where water is available
Date palm (Phoenix dactylifera) — around Lake Chad oases (Bama, Dikwa belts)
Gum arabic (Acacia senegal) — agroforestry stands for export-grade gum
Balanites aegyptiaca (desert date) — edible fruit, oil seed, and medicinal
Acacia nilotica — shade, browse, and tannin tree
Wild melon / egusi-type gourds — drought-resilient minor crops
Roselle (Hibiscus sabdariffa) — zobo drink leaves and calyxes
Sorghum-sudangrass hybrids for fodder in the pastoral system
planting: Plant millet as early as possible once rains establish (late June) — delay causes crop failure in short rainy seasons
Use zaï / tassa pits and half-moons to concentrate scarce runoff water around planting holes
Integrate livestock into crop rotation — penning animals on fields overnight builds soil fertility (korji / dung manuring)
Plant gum arabic (A. senegal) windbreaks across farm fields to reduce wind erosion and diversify income
Rely on indigenous drought-tolerant varieties — avoid hybrids requiring reliable water

name: Oban Hills
summary: Cross River rainforest highlands linked to the Oban sector of Cross River National Park.
description: Oban Hills lie in the Cross River–Cameroon biodiversity hotspot with lowland and montane rainforest, drill monkeys, and forest elephants (rare). Terrain is rugged and heavily forested.
agriculture: Acrisols and ferralsols on steep slopes — highly leached but suitable for tree crops. Land-use pressure is intense outside the park boundary with shifting cultivation and cocoa farms.
crops: Cocoa (Theobroma cacao) — shaded cocoa agroforestry on park buffer-zone farms
Oil palm (Elaeis guineensis) — semi-wild stands and plantation palms
Rubber (Hevea brasiliensis) — smallholder rubber on gentler slopes
Plantain and banana — staple food of the Efik and Ejagham communities
Cassava and yam — shifting-cultivation staples in the wider district
Cocoyam, sweet potato, and taro — under-storey root crops
Okra, pepper, and amaranth — backyard vegetables in the villages
Citrus (oranges, tangerine, lime) — expanding market-garden orchards
Kolanut (Cola nitida & acuminata) — traditional cash crop with ceremonial uses
Bush mango (Irvingia gabonensis) — ogbono soup seeds from retained forest trees
Raffia palm (Raphia spp.) — palm wine, thatch, and raffia fibre
Timber species: mahogany, obeche, iroko — strictly protected inside the national park
planting: Practice agroforestry: retain large native forest trees when planting cocoa — they shade the crop and protect watersheds
Build contour stone lines or grass barriers on hillsides to stop sheet erosion
Rotate cocoa farms with 10–15 year fallows under secondary forest to rebuild soil organic matter
Plant multi-purpose nitrogen-fixing trees (Gliricidia, Albizia) along farm boundaries
Respect park boundaries — avoid clearing new farms inside Cross River National Park

name: Sambisa Forest
summary: Vast woodland–grassland complex south of Maiduguri, historically among Nigeria's largest forest blocks.
description: Sambisa spans southern Borno with open woodland, grassland, and seasonal streams draining toward the Yedseram. It is ecologically important Sahel–Sudan transition habitat, though much of the reserve has been degraded by conflict and land-use change since the 2010s.
character: Open woodland, seasonal streams, Sahel fringe ecology.
economy: Limited ecotourism potential; historically grazing and dry-season farming.

name: Cross River National Park
summary: Nigeria's flagship rainforest park in two sectors — Oban and Okwangwo — in the Cross River biodiversity hotspot.
description: Cross River National Park protects some of West Africa's last intact lowland and montane rainforest. The Oban Hills and Okwangwo sectors harbour drill monkeys, forest elephants, chimpanzees, and exceptional plant diversity on rugged terrain near the Cameroon border.
character: Rainforest, rugged hills, international biodiversity hotspot.

name: Yankari Game Reserve
summary: Bauchi's premier wildlife reserve around Wikki Warm Springs and open savanna woodland.
description: Yankari is one of Nigeria's most visited protected areas, combining Sudan savanna woodland with the Wikki Warm Springs. Elephants, baboons, and antelope remain, though poaching pressure has reduced populations since peak tourism in the 1980s–90s.
character: Savanna woodland, warm springs, safari tourism.

name: Okomu National Park
summary: Edo State rainforest fragment of the Niger Delta–Guinea forest transition.
description: Okomu protects one of the last significant lowland rainforest blocks in western Nigeria. White-throated monkeys, forest buffaloes, and rich birdlife persist amid oil-palm plantation pressures on its boundaries.
character: Lowland rainforest, primate habitat, plantation fringe.

name: Kamuku National Park
summary: Kaduna–Niger border park of savanna woodland, inselbergs, and gallery forest.
description: Kamuku lies on the Kaduna Plateau fringe with rocky outcrops, seasonal streams, and mixed woodland. It forms part of the wider savanna conservation landscape between Birnin Gwari and the FCT.

name: Old Oyo National Park
summary: Oyo–Kwara park preserving savanna around the ruins of the Old Oyo Empire.
description: Old Oyo National Park combines Sudan savanna woodland with archaeological sites of the Oyo Empire capital. Wildlife includes antelope and baboons, while cultural tourism focuses on the ancient city ruins.
character: Savanna woodland, empire ruins, cultural landscape.

name: Kainji Lake National Park
summary: Nigeria's first national park, wrapping Kainji Lake and Borgu Game Reserve woodlands.
description: Created in 1979 around the Kainji Dam reservoir, the park merges lake fisheries, savanna woodland, and the Borgu sector's larger mammals. It remains a reference point for Nigerian protected-area management.
character: Reservoir, savanna woodland, Borgu sector wildlife.

name: Chad Basin National Park
summary: Borno–Yobe park of Chad Basin wetlands, acacia woodland, and seasonal lakes.
description: Chad Basin National Park protects Sahel floodplain and woodland near Lake Chad's former southern edge. Seasonal wetlands attract waterbirds, though drought and insecurity have reduced visitation and monitoring.
character: Sahel woodland, seasonal wetlands, Chad Basin fringe.
economy: Limited tourism; pastoralism in buffer zones.

name: Edumanom Forest Reserve
summary: Bayelsa rainforest block with Nigeria's last known population of Niger Delta red colobus.
description: Edumanom is a critically important Niger Delta rainforest fragment near Nembe. It hosts endangered primates and rich lowland forest biodiversity amid intense oil-industry pressure and community land claims.
elevationNote: Near sea level; freshwater swamp fringe
character: Lowland rainforest, primate refuge, delta ecology.
